newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Divided EU leaders meet on future.
newsitem.headline: Divided EU leaders meet on future.

text.p: European Union leaders, divided even over the need to meet each other, gather in Dublin on Saturday to try to prepare their wealthy Western bloc for an influx of poor countries from the east and Mediterranean.
The leaders are expected to urge negotiators drafting a new treaty to make the Union more efficient to finish their task on schedule next June amidst fears that their discussions have come unstuck.
"The Union must equip itself for the global challenges of the 21st century," Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, the summit host, wrote in a letter inviting his colleagues to Dublin.
He said the leaders should prepare themselves to give political guidance and impetus to the talks, known as the inter-governmental conference (IGC).

The talks, which were launched in March, are designed to reform the EU's institutions and procedures so that it can absorb a dozen or more new members from Estonia in the north through eastern Europe to tiny Malta in the south.

That much is agreed. But the leaders who meet each other for the one-day informal gathering in Ireland's capital on Saturday have numerous differences, not least over how well the IGC talks are going.

France and the European Commission, in particular, have been complaining that the negotiations are bogged down, threatening, according to Commission President Jacques Santer, the future plans for enlargement.
Others, including host Bruton, believe the talks are pretty much where they should be six months into what is likely to be a 15-month exercise.
It was pressure from French President Jacques Chirac, backed by Germany, that led to Saturday's summit -- which many were reluctant to have, fearing it would raise expectations.
Britain, more openly than others, has said it believes the summit to be unnecessary.

Behind the differences lie a series of splits among member states about what direction the IGC, indeed the bloc itself, should be taking. While many see it as a chance for a new move towards political integration, others remain wary.

British Prime Minister John Major's Conservative government is the most vehemently opposed to any further loss of national sovereignty. With his party conference only a few days away, Major will seeking to avoid appearing too conciliatory.

London has been blamed for much of the slow pace of the IGC talks, but officials close to the negotiations say few countries are prepared to take the steps widely accepted as necessary or desirable if the bloc is to expand.

These include taking more decisions by majority vote, cutting the number of European commissioners, ceding sovereignty in areas such as foreign policy and judical affairs and developing an EU-wide defence policy.

France and Germany, the traditional engines of European integration, say they are narrowing their difference on what direction the IGC should take, but they have so far failed to come up with an initiative to break the logjam.

That will come before a second summit in Dublin in December, officials say. The two have been calling for a special clause to be added to the EU treaty to allow some countries to integrate faster than others if they wish.
Many EU countries like the idea of flexibility, but they fear letting it go too far and creating a bloc of first, second and even third class countries.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, meanwhile, has indicated that European integration is a slow process and that not everything has to be done now.

"While there are questions that have to be asked, we don't have to answer them immediately," he said in Dublin on Wednesday. "Let us do the simple basic things that are necessary to lay the groundwork for Europe and then let us tackle the problems."
